newsitem.title: INDIA: Asian workers back from UAE with "baggage of woes".
newsitem.headline: Asian workers back from UAE with "baggage of woes".

text.p: Plane loads of downcast, low-paid workers landed back in their south Asian homelands from the oil rich United Arab Emirates on Tuesday as the last days of the Gulf state's amnesty for illegal workers ticked away.
"I came back to India because I was scared I would be put in prison after the September 30 deadline," Ibrahim, a young man from Tamil Nadu, told Reuters in Bombay.
"Almost all the people I know are trying to leave the country," he said after disembarking his flight from Abu Dhabi.
Between 100,00 and 200,000 others from Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, the Philippines and Sri Lanka are expected to have uprooted from the UAE in the weeks running up to the deadline.
Anyone who stays beyond next Monday could end up with a heavy fine for themselves and their employees, and a possible jail sentence under the Emirates' tough new labour law.
Ibrahim had worked in Abu Dhabi for three years. His companion, Abdul Rashid, worked there making automobile spare parts for two years, but lost his job when his firm retrenched.
"I'm back for good. I only came back because I am jobless," he said as he pushed his belongings on a baggage trolley out of the airport.

The 1970s petro-dollar boom drew millions of Asians to the Gulf to meet the huge demand for labour from Arabs enjoying their new-found wealth. Now that the oil money buys less, the people on the fringes are feeling the effects first and hardest.

"I have returned with shattered dreams and baggage full of woes. I am deep in debt. There is inky darkness in front of me when I think of my future," said Thomas, a young man from a fishing village near Trivandrum in Kerala state who had worked in Dubai for three years.
Some desperate Indians have even returned in small boats across the Arabian Sea.

Dilip, a 24-year-old from the southern state of Kerala, where about half the returning Indians come from, said he paid 25,000 rupees two years ago to get to the Gulf by sea. Now he has come back the same way, huddled with a dozen others in a fishing boat with little food and water.

An Indian Foreign Ministry official in New Delhi said the embassies of the affected countries have asked the UAE authorities for some leeway in repatriating their nationals after the September 30 deadline expires.
India now estimates that just over 40,000 of its people will be repatriated, down from earlier estimates as high as 60,000.
"Processing the documents is no longer a problem, the problem is getting the people out," said the official.
She said Indian airlines were putting on a large number of extra flights to cope with the mass exit. Two ships have also been chartered to ferry around 3,500 Indians home.
Despite a two-month amnesty period, most of the illegal workers appear to have left it to the last few days to get out.
The majority of them had menial jobs as housemaid workers or labourers, often earning too little to afford their own air fares. And most came from the Indian subcontinent.
Bangladesh expects 30,000 of its people will have to restart their lives back home.

"We have been driven away like cats and dogs," Olia Maiah told reporters in Dhaka. "I had worked there for five or six years without any papers, but was suddenly told I was an outlaw and an illegal immigrant."
On Monday, a UAE newspaper reported that almost all the Sri Lankan housemaids had gone home.

A Pakistan Labour Ministry official said about 7,000 Pakistanis were coming from Dubai and hundreds were expected from other emirates. Pakistan airlines have organised an extra 22 flights to the UAE this month to cope.
